It says that if you draw two lines inside a triangle from the ends of one side, those lines will be shorter than the other two sides of the triangle, but the angle they form will be bigger than one of the original angles.

First, I need to understand the setup. There's a triangle ABC, and on side BC, we're constructing two internal lines BD and DC from points B and C. So, BD and DC are inside the triangle, starting from B and C respectively.

The conclusion has two parts: 
1. BD and DC are less than BA and AC. 
2. The angle BDC is greater than angle BAC.

Okay, to formalize this, I need to capture these relationships in Lean 4 code. I'll need to reference points, lines, and angles, so I'll use the provided axioms and definitions.

I'll start by defining the points and lines involved. Point B and C are on line BC, and D is a new point constructed somewhere along BC. BD and DC are segments on BC, so their lengths are parts of BC.

Next, I need to express that BD and DC are less than BA and AC. That means |(b─d)| < |(b─a)| and |(d─c)| < |(a─c)|. 

Then, for the angle part, angle BDC needs to be greater than angle BAC. In Lean, angles are represented with ∠ and their measures are in real numbers. So, ∠ b:d:c should be greater than ∠ b:a:c.

I also need to ensure that all the necessary axioms are used, like twoLinesIntersectAtPoint to establish where the lines intersect, and formTriangle to define the triangle ABC.

I might need to use some geometric theorems or properties here, but since I can't define intermediate variables or use additional operators beyond the basics, I have to stick to the provided axioms and relations.

Potential pitfalls: I need to make sure that D is correctly placed on BC, and that BD and DC are indeed parts of BC. Also, comparing lengths and angles accurately is crucial.

After setting up the hypotheses correctly, I can outline the proof structure, but since I'm just formalizing, I'll end with := by sorry to indicate the placeholder for the actual proof steps.

theorem example_thm (a b c d : Point) (AB BC AC : Line) (h1 : formTriangle a b c AB BC AC) (h2 : twoLinesIntersectAtPoint AB BC b) (h3 : distinctPointsOnLine b c BC) (h4 : twoLinesIntersectAtPoint BC AC c) : |(b─d)| < |(b─a)| ∧ |(d─c)| < |(a─c)| ∧ (∠ b:d:c > ∠ b:a:c) := by sorry
  -- We need to prove that |(b─d)| < |(b─a)|, |(d─c)| < |(a─c)|, and ∠ b:d:c > ∠ b:a:c.
  refine' ⟨_, _, _⟩
  -- Prove |(b─d)| < |(b─a)|
  case refine'_1 =>
    -- Use the fact that D is between B and C on line BC.
    have h5 : between b d c := h1
    -- Use the property of line segments to compare lengths.
    have h6 : |(b─d)| < |(b─a)| := by
      apply Line.length_between_lt
      exact h5
      exact h2
    exact h6
  -- Prove |(d─c)| < |(a─c)|
  case refine'_2 =>
    -- Use the fact that D is between B and C on line BC.
    have h5 : between b d c := h1
    -- Use the property of line segments to compare lengths.
    have h7 : |(d─c)| < |(a─c)| := by
      apply Line.length_between_lt
      exact h5
      exact h4
    exact h7
  -- Prove ∠ b:d:c > ∠ b:a:c
  case refine'_3 =>
    -- Use the property of angles formed by intersecting lines.
    have h8 : ∠ b:d:c > ∠ b:a:c := by
      apply Angle.angle_between_greater
      exact h3
      exact h2
      exact h4
    exact h8

nl_statement: If two internal straight-lines are constructed on one of the sides of a triangle, from its ends, the constructed (straight-lines) will be less than the two remaining  sides of the triangle, but will encompass a greater angle. For let the two internal straight-lines $BD$ and $DC$ have been constructed on one of the sides $BC$ of the triangle $ABC$, from its ends $B$ and $C$ (respectively). I say that  $BD$ and $DC$ are less than the (sum of the) two  remaining sides of the triangle $BA$ and $AC$, but encompass an angle $BDC$ greater than $BAC$.    <prf>  Thus, $BDC$ is much greater than $BAC$.Thus, if two internal straight-lines are constructed on one of the sides of a triangle, from its ends,  the constructed (straight-lines) are less than the two remaining  sides of the triangle, but  encompass a greater angle.
